blocks.text: **The problem.** Like House Robber, but the houses stand in a **circle**: the first and the last house are neighbours too. Return the most you can rob without robbing two adjacent houses.

blocks.alt: nums is 2, 3, 2 in a circle. The first and last houses touch, so they can't both be robbed. Split into two straight streets: without the last house, 2 and 3, the best is 3; without the first house, 3 and 2, the best is 3. The answer is the larger, 3.

elements.text: first and last are neighbours: never rob both, so solve two straight streets

blocks.text: The only new rule is that houses `0` and `n − 1` can't both be robbed. So in any valid plan, at least one of them is skipped. Solve House Robber twice on straight streets — once on houses `0..n−2` (the last one skipped) and once on `1..n−1` (the first one skipped) — and take the larger. Each straight street is the previous lesson's O(1)-space loop.
1. Remember whether the first house was robbed
The recursion carries one extra flag — was house 0 robbed? If so, the last house is off limits. Memoize on (house, flag).
**Time O(n), space O(n).** Correct, but the extra flag makes it fiddly.

blocks.caption: Run House Robber on the street without the last house, then without the first, and keep the better.

blocks.text: **Time O(n), space O(1).** Two linear passes.

blocks.alt: Flag + memo: O(n) time, O(n) space. Two straight streets: O(n) time, O(1) space.

items: **One house** — both streets would be empty; return `nums[0]` directly.
**Three equal houses** — only one can be robbed.
**Pizza With 3n Slices** — a circle again: solve twice, without the first and without the last.
**Circular maximum subarray** — the same "break the circle" idea for Kadane's algorithm.
